subcards.title: Political concepts and theory
subcards.summary: Basic political science ideas: State, sovereignty, democracy, constitutionalism and key thinkers.
at_a_glance: Four elements: population, territory, government, sovereignty
The supreme power of the State; the key thinkers are Jean Bodin and John Austin
Government limited by law; its opposite is despotism (unlimited, arbitrary rule)
Explained by A.V. Dicey; India accepts 2 of his 3 elements
Given by Montesquieu in his book The Spirit of Laws (1748)
Citizens decide directly through referendum, initiative, recall and plebiscite; Switzerland uses it
Both aim, in the end, at a society without the State (stateless society)
Covers 143 countries; Denmark is first and Venezuela is last (as of Nov 2026)

sections.heading: The State and its four elements

blocks.text: The State is a group of people, politically organised, living on a definite territory, having its own government and not controlled by any outside power. The State is an abstract idea (you cannot see or touch it); it shows itself through its government.

blocks.title: Four essential elements of the State
head: Element
Meaning
rows: The people who live in the State and form it
A definite area over which the State has control
The agency (machinery) through which the will of the State is expressed and carried out
Supreme power. Internal: power over everyone inside the State. External: freedom from control by any outside power

blocks.title: State vs government
head: Aspect
State
Government
rows: Concrete (it can be seen); it is only one element of the State
Does not own sovereignty; it only uses it on behalf of the State

blocks.title: Best definition of the State (UPSC 2021 answer)
items: 'A community of persons permanently occupying a definite territory, independent of external control and possessing an organised government.' This definition covers all four elements: people, territory, government and sovereignty.
Andhra Pradesh is called a 'State' in the Constitution of India, but in political science it is not a State, because it does not have sovereignty.

blocks.title: Kinds of sovereignty
head: Kind
Meaning
rows: The authority whose commands (laws) are enforced by the courts — for example, Parliament
The voters and public opinion that stand behind the law-maker and influence it
The people are the final source of all authority; democracy rests on this idea
Real power that people actually obey, even though it has no legal right to rule (for example, a group that takes power in a coup)

blocks.title: Thinkers on sovereignty and law
head: Thinker
Idea
rows: Sovereignty is supreme power over citizens and subjects, and it is not limited by law
Sovereignty is the command of a 'determinate superior' (a definite person or body) whom people habitually obey. This is legal sovereignty
Rule of law (everyone is under the same law)
Separation of powers (law-making, executing and judging kept in different hands)

blocks.title: Direct vs representative democracy
head: Aspect
Direct democracy
Representative democracy
rows: Elected representatives make laws and govern
Switzerland uses referendum and popular initiative at the federal level

blocks.title: Devices of direct democracy
head: Device
What it does
rows: Voters themselves decide a law or a policy question by voting on it
Citizens themselves put forward a proposal for a law
Voters remove an elected representative before the end of the term
A popular vote to find public opinion on an important political question (e.g. which country a territory should join)
blocks.note: The Constitution of India does NOT need a referendum (vote of the people) to pass a constitutional amendment. Under Article 368, only Parliament passes it; for some amendments, half of the State Legislatures must also agree.

blocks.title: Democracy — points from previous exam questions
items: Statement: in a democracy, the final responsibility of administration is to the people. Reason: democracy rests on popular sovereignty (the people are the source of all power). Both are true, and the reason correctly explains the statement.
The superior virtue (greatest merit) of democracy: it calls into activity the intelligence and character of ordinary men and women (UPSC 2017).
Hallmark (most distinctive sign) of democracy: freedom of speech and expression.
Democracy helps development because it encourages citizen participation and accountability.
All democratic countries are likely to have a constitution (NCERT).

blocks.title: Meaning of constitution
items: The word 'constitution' comes from the Latin word 'constituere', which means 'to establish' or 'to set up'.
A constitution is the fundamental (highest) law. It sets out the structure of government, its powers, the rights of people and the relationship between government and people.
It is called an 'organic law' because it sets up the basic organisation and framework of the government.
Ordinary laws must stay within the limits set by the constitution.

blocks.title: Functions of a constitution (NCERT)
head: Function
Meaning
rows: Gives basic rules that allow the members of a diverse society to live and work together and to trust each other
Says who has power to make decisions and how the government is formed
Defines and limits the powers of government. UPSC treats this as the chief purpose of a constitution
Enables the government to work towards a just society and fulfil the people's social and economic goals
Guarantees a set of rights to citizens, and gives the courts a standard to test laws (judicial review)
blocks.note: NOT a function of a constitution: 'to ensure participation of good people in politics'.

blocks.title: Constitution vs constitutionalism (Laxmikanth)
head: Aspect
Constitution
Constitutionalism
rows: A document of basic rules (it may be written in one document or not)
The idea of limited government under law
Can one exist without the other?
Yes — a dictatorship may have a written constitution but still no constitutionalism
Needs real, effective limits on power, not just a document. The UK has constitutionalism without a single written constitution

blocks.title: Definitions to remember
head: Who
Said
rows: Constitutionalism is a system of effective restraints on government action
Constitutionalism essentially means limited government; it is the opposite of rule by the unlimited will of the rulers
A constitutional government places effective limits on the authority of the State in order to protect individual liberty (not limits on liberty in order to protect State authority)

blocks.title: Dicey's rule of law — 3 elements
head: Element
Applies in India?
rows: 1. Absence of arbitrary power: no one can be punished except for breaking a law
2. Equality before law: everyone, rich or poor, government official or ordinary person, is under the same ordinary law and the same ordinary courts
3. Primacy of individual rights: the constitution is the RESULT of rights already recognised by the courts
No — in India it is the other way round: the Constitution itself is the SOURCE of rights
blocks.note: Dicey's book: Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution (1885).

blocks.title: Constitutional morality and rule-of-law ranking
items: B.R. Ambedkar spoke about constitutional morality (respect for the Constitution's spirit and its limits) while introducing the Draft Constitution in the Constituent Assembly on 4 November 1948. He said: 'Constitutional morality is not a natural sentiment. It has to be cultivated.'

WJP Rule of Law Index 2026 (released by the World Justice Project in October 2026): it covered 143 countries and jurisdictions. Denmark was ranked first and Venezuela last. Finland was NOT first (as of Nov 2026).

sections.heading: Separation of powers and checks and balances

blocks.title: Theory
items: Given by Montesquieu, a French thinker, in The Spirit of Laws (1748).
Purpose: to protect liberty by keeping the three powers (making laws, carrying them out and judging) in different hands. Separation of powers is called the best safeguard of liberty.
His model was the British constitution, NOT the US Congress (the US Constitution was written later, in 1787).

blocks.title: Three organs
head: Organ
Main function
Article (India)
rows: Decides disputes (adjudication); protects rights and examines whether laws and orders are valid

blocks.title: Political vs permanent executive
head: Aspect
Political executive
Permanent executive
rows: Stay in office only as long as they have the confidence (majority support) of the legislature
Continue even when the government changes

blocks.title: Checks and balances (one branch restrains another)
head: Device
Who checks whom
rows: Judicial review of an Act (court can strike down a law)
Removal of judges by an address (special motion) of Parliament
President withholding assent to a Bill (executive veto — refusing to sign)
US Senate must consent to certain presidential appointments; a treaty needs the approval of two-thirds of the senators present
blocks.note: Example: a court strikes down a law, and the legislature then passes a revised law within constitutional limits. This shows checks with functional interdependence — each organ checks the other, yet they depend on each other to do the work.

blocks.title: India: no rigid separation
head: Case (year)
Held
Why it matters
rows: India has no rigid separation of powers. Executive power is residual: it is whatever remains after legislative and judicial functions are taken away
Explains how the Indian model works
The President and the Governor must act on the advice of their ministers
Real power lies with the Council of Ministers
Parliament cannot alter the basic structure of the Constitution
Puts a limit on Parliament's amending power
Parliament's limited power to amend is itself a basic feature of the Constitution
Puts a limit on Parliament's amending power

blocks.title: India — related points
items: Article 50 (a Directive Principle) asks the State to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services. This is true, but it does not explain why the legislature and the executive are not separated — in a parliamentary system they are joined (fused), because ministers are members of the legislature.
Delegation: a grant of power to a subordinate that can be taken back (revocable). Devolution: a legal transfer of power to local bodies by a law (statute).
The 73rd Amendment gives the framework for devolution to rural local bodies (panchayats); the 74th Amendment does the same for urban local bodies (municipalities).

sections.heading: Forms of government and other countries' systems

blocks.title: Aristotle's classification of governments (in his book Politics)
head: Rulers
True form (rulers rule for the common good)
Perverted form (rulers rule for themselves)
blocks.note: Aristotle classified governments by two tests: the number of rulers, and whether they rule for the common interest or for their own.

blocks.title: UK's uncodified constitution (not in one single document) — key documents

items.what: Magna Carta
items.detail: Limited the arbitrary (unchecked) power of the King

items.what: Bill of Rights
items.detail: Established that Parliament is supreme over the Crown (the monarch)

items.what: Parliament Act
items.detail: Reduced the veto power (power to block Bills) of the House of Lords

items.what: Human Rights Act
Constitutional Reform Act
items.detail: Created the Supreme Court of the United Kingdom

blocks.title: Legislatures of other countries
head: Country
Upper house
Lower house
rows: No upper house — unicameral (one chamber): National People's Congress
blocks.note: Bicameral = two chambers; unicameral = one chamber. Trap: the US Senate is the UPPER house, not the lower house.

blocks.title: France (Constitution of 1958)
items: The Prime Minister directs the actions of the Government.
The Government is responsible (answerable) to Parliament under the conditions laid down in the Constitution.

sections.heading: Ideologies: Marxism, Gandhism, anarchism, fascism, welfare state

blocks.title: Marxism vs Gandhism
head: Aspect
Marxism
Gandhism
rows: Class struggle (conflict between rich and poor classes), economic interpretation of history, classless society
Non-violence, trusteeship (the rich hold wealth in trust for society), decentralisation
Stateless society (the State 'withers away', that is, slowly disappears)
Stateless society (enlightened anarchy — people govern themselves without a State)
blocks.note: The ONE point common to both: the final goal of a stateless society (UPSC 2020).

blocks.title: Other ideologies
head: Ideology
Meaning
rows: Society organised without the State. Anarchists say the State rests on force (coercion), so it causes social evils. Replacing one ruler with another is not enough; voluntary cooperation should replace authority imposed from above
Led by Mussolini (Italy); it suppresses opposition and dissent
Led by Hitler (Germany). Hitler wrote Mein Kampf (not Mussolini)
Aims to REDUCE the concentration of wealth in a few hands (not increase it)
French for 'let it be' — the State should interfere as little as possible in markets
The State runs public programmes for the broad well-being of society. It does more than a 'police state', which only keeps order and provides security and defence
Extending control over other countries or territories

blocks.title: Anarchist thinkers
head: Thinker
Work
Idea
rows: Called himself an anarchist in this book
COOPERATION (not competition) is the main factor in the evolution (development) of society

blocks.title: Globalisation vs crony capitalism
head: Aspect
Globalisation
Crony capitalism
rows: Economic integration (linking) of countries; countries may change their economic policies to follow world trends
Businesses gain advantages through political connections and favours from the government
Is NOT open competition based on rules

items: Inclusive development in Indian governance means welfare schemes that target all sections of society.

blocks.title: Thinkers and books
head: Author
Book
rows: Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution
Some Characteristics of the Indian Constitution (1953)
The Indian Constitution: Cornerstone of a Nation (1966). He called the Constitution 'first and foremost a social document'
Introduction to the Constitution of India
An Introduction to the Constitution of India
Asian Drama — gave the idea of the 'soft state' (a State that is weak in enforcing its own rules and policies)
Cabbages and Kings — the book that coined the term 'banana republic'
Study of bureaucracy (a system run by appointed officials)

blocks.title: Political terms
head: Term
Meaning
rows: An official government statement of information or policy
Too much procedure and delay in administration. The name comes from clerks tying bundles of files with red tape. It does NOT mean that every safeguard is useless
Can mean social media, in public discussion
Groups outside the government (such as NGOs). It helps good governance by getting people to take part in public affairs and by improving transparency
Russian for 'openness' — the policy of Mikhail Gorbachev in the USSR
A sudden seizure of government power

Latin for 'unwelcome person' — a diplomat who is no longer accepted. Under Article 9 of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, only the RECEIVING state (the host country) declares it, at any time and without giving reasons

An unstable country that depends on one export and is run for a small rich group (elite). The term does not describe any formal constitutional design. Exporting farm goods alone does not make a country a banana republic
Latin for 'parent of the nation' — the State acts as the legal protector of people who cannot protect themselves
Latin for 'hear the other side' — the right to be heard before a decision is taken (a rule of natural justice, that is, fair procedure)

items: Andhra Pradesh is a 'State' in the Constitution but not in political science, because it has no sovereignty.
The opposite of constitutionalism is despotism (not federalism, pluralism or socialism).
Dicey's 3rd element does not apply to India, because our Constitution is the source of rights.
Montesquieu based his theory on the British constitution, not on the US Congress.
Only the receiving (host) state can declare a diplomat persona non grata (unwelcome).
Mein Kampf was written by Hitler, not Mussolini. The US Senate is the upper house. China's legislature has only one chamber.
Kropotkin's Mutual Aid stresses cooperation, not competition.
India needs no referendum to amend its Constitution; Switzerland uses referendum and popular initiative.

subcards.title: Civil Services (Part XIV, Art 308–323)
subcards.summary: How civil servants are recruited, protected, controlled, and reformed in India.
at_a_glance: Part XIV — Articles 308 to 323 (services 308–314; Public Service Commissions 315–323)
All-India Services, Central Services, State Services
3 — Indian Administrative Service (IAS), Indian Police Service (IPS) and Indian Forest Service (IFoS, the third one, started in 1966)
Article 310 — civil servants hold office at the pleasure of the President or Governor
Article 311 — an officer cannot be dismissed by an authority lower than the one that appointed him or her, and an inquiry with a chance to be heard must come first
Article 312 — first Rajya Sabha passes a resolution supported by two-thirds of members present and voting, then Parliament makes a law
Articles 323A and 323B were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976). The Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) was set up in 1985.
Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel. Civil Services Day is celebrated on 21 April.

blocks.title: All-India vs Central vs State Services
head: Aspect
All-India Services
Central Services
State Services
rows: Both the Centre and the states, by turns
Indian Foreign Service, Indian Revenue Service, Indian Audit and Accounts Service, Indian Economic Service, Central Engineering Service
State civil (administrative) service, state police service, state forest service, state medical service, state judicial service
Shared (joint): final (ultimate) control is with the Centre; day-to-day (immediate) control is with the state
The state where the officer serves

blocks.title: Key facts
items: Indian Foreign Service is a Central Service, NOT an All-India Service. It is the top Central Service; it ranks next to IAS and its pay is higher than IPS. It is run by the Ministry of External Affairs.

Central Services are grouped as Group A, Group B, Group C and Group D. Until 1974 they were called Class I, II, III and IV; the names were changed in 1974 on the advice of the Third Pay Commission. Group A and Group B posts are 'gazetted' (appointments are published in the official Government Gazette); Group C and Group D are not.
Laxmikanth lists 66 Group A Central Services at present.
Up to one-third (33⅓ per cent) of senior posts in the IAS, IPS and Indian Forest Service are filled by promoting officers of the state services (under the All-India Services Act, 1951).

blocks.title: Articles at a glance
head: Article
What it says
rows: Meaning of terms used in this Part

Parliament (for Central employees) and state legislatures (for state employees) make laws on recruitment and conditions of service. Until such a law is made, the President (for the Centre) or the Governor (for a state) makes the rules. This is the 'proviso' (an added condition) to Art 309.
Doctrine of pleasure: civil servants of the Centre, All-India Services and defence services hold office at the pleasure of the President; state civil servants at the pleasure of the Governor.
Gives two protections (safeguards) to civil servants that limit the doctrine of pleasure in Art 310 (see below)
Allows Parliament to create new All-India Services, including an All-India Judicial Service
Added by the 28th Amendment (1972). Parliament can change or cancel the service conditions of officers appointed by the British Crown before 1950 (the old Indian Civil Service, ICS, officers).
Transitional (temporary) rule: service laws in force before 1950 continue until they are changed
Gave protection to officers already in service in 1950 — this Article was repealed (removed) by the 28th Amendment (1972)

blocks.title: Art 309 — recruitment and conditions of service
items: 'Recruitment' includes appointment, selection, deputation, promotion and transfer.
'Conditions of service' include pay, leave, promotion, transfer, disciplinary action, retirement and pension.

Under Art 309, the law can put reasonable limits on the Fundamental Rights of civil servants, to keep them honest (integrity), disciplined, neutral and able to keep secrets. These limits are written in conduct rules, such as the Central Services (Conduct) Rules.
So civil servants face strict limits on political activity (they cannot join parties or campaign), but they still have the right to vote.

blocks.title: Art 310 — doctrine of pleasure
items: It comes from British practice (English common law): a servant of the Crown (the King or Queen) could be removed whenever the Crown wished — 'at the Crown's pleasure'.
It is NOT absolute (unlimited) in India: Art 311 limits it. So a civil servant cannot be removed just at the government's wish; the Art 311 safeguards must be followed.

Exception: to hire a person with special skills, the government can sign a contract that promises payment (compensation) if the post is abolished before the contract ends, or if the person has to leave for reasons other than his or her own misconduct. Only a person newly joining service can get such a contract.

blocks.title: Art 311 — two safeguards
items: 1. A civil servant cannot be dismissed or removed by an authority lower (subordinate) than the one that appointed him or her.
2. He or she cannot be dismissed, removed or reduced in rank without an inquiry. In the inquiry, the officer must be told the charges and given a reasonable chance to be heard.
These safeguards cover civil servants only. They do not cover members of the defence services or holders of military posts.
Difference: a dismissed person cannot get a government job in future; a removed person can.

blocks.title: When the inquiry (safeguard 2) can be skipped
head: Case
Who decides
rows: The officer is convicted (found guilty) on a criminal charge
No separate decision needed — the conviction itself is the ground
Holding an inquiry is not reasonably practicable (not possible in practice); the reasons must be recorded in writing
The authority that has the power to dismiss the officer
Holding an inquiry is not expedient (not advisable) in the interest of the security of the state

blocks.text: The 42nd Amendment (1976) removed the 'second opportunity'. Earlier, after the inquiry, the officer got a second chance to object to the proposed punishment. Now the hearing is given only once, at the inquiry stage.

blocks.title: Art 323A vs Art 323B
head: Aspect
Art 323A
Art 323B
rows: Only service matters (recruitment and conditions of service of public servants)
Other matters, such as tax, land reforms, elections and industrial disputes

blocks.title: Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT)
items: Set up in 1985 under the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985. Its principal (main) bench is at New Delhi, and it has 19 regular benches.

It covers All-India Services, Central civil services and civilian (non-uniformed) employees of the defence services. It does NOT cover members of the defence forces, staff of the Supreme Court, or the secretariat staff of Parliament.
It does not have to follow the Civil Procedure Code (the detailed rules courts follow); it follows the principles of natural justice (a fair hearing for both sides). The application fee is only ₹50.

L. Chandra Kumar case (1997): earlier, the law did not allow High Courts to hear cases against CAT orders. The Supreme Court struck down this bar, because judicial review (the courts' power to check government action) is part of the basic structure of the Constitution. Now an appeal against a CAT order goes first to a division bench (two or more judges) of the High Court, not straight to the Supreme Court.

blocks.text: See the Tribunals card for full details

items.what: The Indian Civil Service (ICS) was replaced by the IAS, and the Indian Police (IP) was replaced by the IPS
IAS and IPS were treated as (deemed to be) services created by Parliament under Art 312
All-India Services Act passed — it lets the Centre make rules, after consulting the states, on recruitment and conditions of service
A law provided for three new services: Indian Forest Service, Indian Medical and Health Service, and Indian Service of Engineers
Only the Indian Forest Service actually came into existence — the third All-India Service
The 42nd Amendment made provision for an All-India Judicial Service — but no law has been made to create it so far

blocks.title: Art 312 — creating a new All-India Service
items: Step 1: Rajya Sabha passes a resolution, supported by two-thirds of members present and voting, that the service is needed in the national interest.
Step 2: Parliament makes a law creating it. A Rajya Sabha resolution alone does not create the service.
Why Rajya Sabha: it represents the states, so this protects state interests in the federal system.
Lok Sabha and state assemblies have no such role.

An All-India Judicial Service cannot include any post below the rank of district judge. A law creating it is NOT treated as an amendment of the Constitution under Art 368 (so it can be passed like an ordinary law).

In Art 312, the All-India Judicial Service is named in the main clause, and IAS and IPS are mentioned in clause (2), Art 312(2). It does not name any 'Security Service' or the Indian Forest Service. So the services mentioned in the Constitution are IAS, IPS and the All-India Judicial Service.

blocks.title: Control and discipline
items: Their conditions of service are set by Parliament (through Art 312 and the All-India Services Act, 1951) — not directly by the President, the Constitution or the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC).

Officers are recruited and trained by the Centre, then given a state cadre (the state group of posts they belong to). The Centre has no cadre of its own; officers go to the Centre on deputation for a fixed period (the tenure system) and then return to their state.
Control is shared (joint): final (ultimate) control is with the Centre; immediate (day-to-day) control is with the state.
Disciplinary action (punishments), including dismissal, can be taken only by the Central Government — even for an IAS officer working in a state.

The President appoints these officers. So an officer can appeal to the President against an order of a state government. Art 311 also says an officer cannot be removed by an authority lower than the one that appointed him or her.
There are 26 state cadres. Two of them are joint cadres shared by more than one state: (1) Assam and Meghalaya, and (2) AGMUT (Arunachal Pradesh, Goa, Mizoram and the Union Territories).
Ministries in charge: the IAS is managed by the Ministry of Personnel; the IPS by the Ministry of Home Affairs; the Indian Forest Service by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change.
All-India Services are seen as tools of national integration (keeping the country united), because officers appointed by the President work in all states under the same rules and pay.

blocks.title: Who called them what
head: Person
Idea
rows: 'Father of All-India Services' — he pushed for them in the Constituent Assembly (the Draft Constitution had not mentioned them). He called the civil services the 'steel frame' of India.
21 April — on this day in 1947, Patel addressed the first batch of officers (probationers) at Metcalfe House, Delhi

sections.heading: Who runs the government: ministers and civil servants

blocks.title: Political vs permanent executive
head: Aspect
Minister
Secretary (civil servant)
rows: Political head of the ministry — decides policy
Administrative head of the ministry — advises and carries out policy
Temporary — can change after every election
Permanent — stays in service; part of the 'permanent executive'

items: 'Permanent executive' means permanent civil servants who run day-to-day administration.
Main role of the bureaucracy (the body of civil servants) in India: an agency for carrying out (implementing) public policy.

Under the proviso (added condition) of Art 309, the President makes service rules for Union employees until Parliament makes a law. Compare other Articles: Art 145 — the Supreme Court frames its own rules; Art 61 — Parliament tries the President through impeachment; Art 323A — administrative tribunals settle service disputes.

blocks.title: Models of district administration (after independence)
head: Model
Idea
rows: Keep regulatory work (law and order, revenue collection) separate from development work
Combine regulatory work and development work under the District Collector
blocks.note: A previous-year exam question says a 'third model was recommended by the Sarkaria Commission'. That statement is wrong — the Sarkaria Commission (1983–88) dealt with Centre–state relations, not district administration.

items.what: Macaulay Committee
items.detail: First recommended selecting civil servants through an open competitive examination

items.what: D.S. Kothari Committee
items.detail: A single exam for both All-India and Central services; a preliminary screening test before the main exam. The three stages (prelims, mains, interview) began in 1979.

items.what: Satish Chandra Committee
items.detail: Recommended an essay paper in the main exam (it suggested 250 marks); the essay paper was brought in from the 1993 exam with 200 marks

items.what: Y.K. Alagh Committee
items.detail: An aptitude test in the preliminary exam; fewer optional subjects

items.what: P.C. Hota Committee
items.detail: Entry age 21–24 (relaxation 5 years SC/ST, 3 years OBC); a strict review of civil servants' performance after 15 years of service

items.what: Arun Nigvekar Committee
items.detail: Studied the exam pattern after CSAT (Civil Services Aptitude Test, the aptitude paper in prelims) was introduced

blocks.title: Early administrative reform bodies
items: N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar gave a report (1949) on reorganising the machinery of the Central Government. A UPSC 2021 question said this committee suggested 'a minister and a secretary only for administrative reform' — that statement was treated as wrong.
First Administrative Reforms Commission (1966): first chaired by Morarji Desai, and later by K. Hanumanthaiah.

On this Commission's advice, the Department of Personnel was created in 1970 and placed under the Prime Minister. Today it is the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT), the central agency for government staff matters.
Set up on 31 August 2005 as a Commission of Inquiry, to prepare a detailed plan (blueprint) for reforming public administration.
Chairman: Veerappa Moily. After he resigned in April 2009, V. Ramachandran became chairman.
Submitted 15 reports (2005–2009).

blocks.title: Reports and key recommendations
head: No.
Report
Key recommendation
rows: Right to Information: Master Key to Good Governance

Corrupt public servants must pay for the loss they cause (damages); protect whistle-blowers (people who expose corruption); abolish MPLADS and MLALADS (local-area funds that MPs and MLAs decide how to spend)
All police officers and staff to get a minimum tenure of 3 years; Metropolitan Police Authorities for every city with more than 10 lakh (1 million) people
Octroi (local entry tax on goods) — after this report, all states except Maharashtra abolished octroi (Government reply in Lok Sabha, 2011)
Refurbishing of Personnel Administration – Scaling New Heights
Promoting e-Governance: The Smart Way Forward
Move all dealings between government and citizens to e-governance (online services) by 2020
Citizen Centric Administration: The Heart of Governance
Single-window agencies (one office for all approvals); social audit (checking by the people) made compulsory; Citizen's Charters
A collegium (a small selection group: a minister chosen by the Chief Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and the serving Chief Secretary) to recommend a panel of names for the Chief Secretary

blocks.title: Citizen's Charter and e-governance
items: A Citizen's Charter promises that services will be delivered within a fixed time, and also gives a way to settle complaints (grievance redress).
Technology in e-governance is meant to improve service delivery and citizen engagement — not to replace all human contact.

blocks.text: Lateral entry (outside experts joining at senior levels) above Joint Secretary level was also suggested by the National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution (chaired by M.N. Venkatachaliah, 2000–02).

sections.heading: New reforms: Mission Karmayogi and lateral entry

blocks.title: Mission Karmayogi (National Programme for Civil Services Capacity Building)
items: Approved by the Union Cabinet in September 2020 to train civil servants throughout their careers.

It rests on SIX pillars (not eight): (1) Policy Framework; (2) Institutional Framework; (3) Competency Framework; (4) Digital Learning Framework (the iGOT-Karmayogi online learning platform); (5) electronic Human Resource Management System (e-HRMS); (6) Monitoring and Evaluation Framework.
Status (as of Nov 2026): continuing; training is delivered online through the iGOT-Karmayogi platform.

blocks.title: Lateral entry (outside experts joining at senior levels)

items.what: Lateral recruitment began for Joint Secretary, Director and Deputy Secretary posts
UPSC advertised 45 posts (10 Joint Secretary, 35 Director or Deputy Secretary)
After protests that these posts had no reservation (quota), the Centre asked UPSC to cancel the advertisement; UPSC cancelled it
Government told Rajya Sabha: 63 appointments made through lateral entry since 2018
Lateral entry is on hold; the government said it has not yet found a workable option (as of November 2026, no new advertisement has been found)

items: Indian Foreign Service is a Central Service, not an All-India Service. The third All-India Service is the Indian Forest Service (1966).
Doctrine of pleasure is in Art 310; the safeguards are in Art 311. Art 311 limits Art 310, so the President's or Governor's 'pleasure' is not absolute.
A new All-India Service needs a Rajya Sabha resolution (two-thirds present and voting) AND a law of Parliament.
Service conditions of All-India Services are fixed by Parliament (All-India Services Act, 1951).
Only the Centre can dismiss an All-India Service officer, even one working in a state.
Constitution mentions IAS, IPS and All-India Judicial Service — not IFoS or Indian Foreign Service.
Civil servants cannot take part in party politics, but they can vote.
Mission Karmayogi has six pillars. The Second Administrative Reforms Commission gave 15 reports; the 10th report is on personnel administration.

subcards.title: GST Council (Art 279A) and GST
subcards.summary: Who sits in the GST Council, how it votes, and what it recommends.
at_a_glance: By an order of the President dated 15 September 2016. Art 279A(1) gave the President 60 days to do this.
33: 2 from the Union and 31 from States and the UTs that have a legislature (Delhi, Puducherry, Jammu and Kashmir)
A decision needs three-fourths of the weighted votes of members present and voting. The Centre's vote counts for one-third; all States together count for two-thirds.
Constitutional body; its recommendations are not binding (Mohit Minerals case, 2022)
Two main rates (slabs), 5% and 18%, plus a 40% rate for luxury and 'sin' (harmful) goods, from 22 September 2025

sections.heading: What GST is and how the Council was set up

head: Point
Fact
rows: One tax on the supply of goods and services. It replaced many old indirect taxes of the Centre and the States.
The tax money goes to the State where the goods or services are finally used (consumed), not to the State where they are made. GST is an indirect tax, not a direct tax.
101st Amendment Act, 2016 (it was the 122nd Amendment Bill). It added Art 246A (power to make GST laws), Art 269A (inter-State GST) and Art 279A (GST Council).

Assam was the first State to ratify (approve) the GST Amendment Bill, in August 2016. The Bill needed approval by the legislatures of at least half the States, because it changed Centre–State relations.
The President had to set up the GST Council within 60 days from the date the 101st Amendment Act came into force
By a Presidential order dated 15 September 2016
22–23 September 2016, in New Delhi, chaired by Union Finance Minister Arun Jaitley

blocks.text: For Art 246A, Art 269A, the types of GST (CGST, SGST, UTGST, IGST) and the old taxes merged into GST, see Financial relations

sections.heading: Who sits in the GST Council

blocks.title: Composition (Art 279A(2))
head: Position
Who holds it
rows: Union Finance Minister (not the Prime Minister, not the President)
Union Minister of State in charge of Revenue or Finance

The Finance or Taxation Minister, or any other Minister, nominated by each State government. Delhi, Puducherry and Jammu and Kashmir count as 'States' here (Art 366(26B)), because they have a legislature.
Chosen by the State members from among themselves. The State members also decide his or her term. The Union members do not vote in this choice, and the Constitution fixes no term.
33 members: 2 Union members and 31 State members (28 States and 3 UTs with a legislature)

blocks.title: Not voting members
head: Who
Position
rows: Chairperson of the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC)
Permanent invitee to all meetings, but with no vote. This was added by a Union Cabinet decision, not by Art 279A. So the CBIC Chairperson is not counted in weighted voting.
Ex-officio Secretary of the Council (holds this post because of his or her government post). Not a member.
Ladakh, Andaman and Nicobar, Chandigarh and other UTs without a legislature
Not members, because they have no legislature. In these UTs, GST is collected as UTGST (Union Territory GST) under a law made by Parliament.

head: Rule
Fact
rows: Quorum (minimum members present for a valid meeting) — Art 279A(7)
One-half of total members. With 33 members, at least 17 must be present.
At least three-fourths (75%) of the weighted votes of members present and voting. It is NOT a simple majority and NOT two-thirds.
One-third (about 33%) of the total votes cast in the meeting
Two-thirds (about 67%) of the total votes cast in the meeting. So the States together have twice the weight of the Centre.

steps.step: Centre votes NO, all States vote YES
steps.detail: YES = two-thirds (67%), which is less than three-fourths (75%). The proposal FAILS. So the States alone cannot pass a decision.

steps.step: Centre votes YES alone, States vote NO
steps.detail: YES = one-third (33%). The proposal FAILS. So the Centre alone cannot pass a decision either.

steps.step: Centre votes YES: how much State support is needed?
steps.detail: The proposal needs three-fourths (3/4) of the total. The Centre gives one-third (1/3). So the States must add 3/4 − 1/3 = 5/12 of the total. The States' full share is 2/3 (= 8/12), so they must give 5 out of their 8 parts, that is 5/8 or 62.5% of the States' combined vote.

A decision fails if more than one-fourth (25%) of the weighted vote is NO. The Centre alone can block, because its 33% is more than 25%. A large group of States can also block, if together they hold more than 25% of the total votes (that is, more than 3/8 of the States' share).

blocks.title: Acts that stay valid — Art 279A(10)
head: A Council decision is NOT invalid merely because of
Note
rows: A vacancy or a defect in how the Council is formed
A defect in the appointment of a member
A procedural mistake that does not affect the merits of the case
A decision taken WITHOUT the required three-fourths weighted majority
NOT protected. Such a decision is not valid.

blocks.text: Art 279A(6): in its work the Council must be guided by the need for a harmonised (uniform) GST structure and a harmonised national market for goods and services. Art 279A(8): the Council itself decides its own procedure (Parliament does not lay it down).

blocks.title: Vision and mission (Laxmikanth)
head: Item
Text
rows: To set the highest standards of co-operative federalism (the Centre and the States working together) in the Council's work. It calls the Council the 'first constitutional federal body' with power to take all major decisions on GST.
To build, through wider consultation, a GST structure that is information-technology-driven (run on computers and online systems) and user-friendly

blocks.title: Recommendations to the Centre and the States — Art 279A(4)
items: (a) Which taxes, cesses and surcharges of the Centre, the States and local bodies will merge into GST
(b) Which goods and services will pay GST and which will be exempted

(c) Model GST laws; principles of levy (basic rules on how GST is charged); how GST on inter-State trade (IGST) is shared between the Centre and States; and place-of-supply rules (rules that decide in which State a supply is taxed)
(d) The threshold turnover limit: the yearly sales below which a supplier may be exempted from GST
(e) GST rates, including floor rates (minimum rates) with bands (a permitted range above the floor rate)
(f) Special rates for a fixed period to raise extra money during a natural calamity or disaster

(g) Special provisions for 11 States: Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Jammu and Kashmir, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim, Tripura, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand (Andhra Pradesh is NOT in this list)
(h) Any other GST matter the Council decides

blocks.title: Other functions
items: Art 279A(5): the Council recommends the date from which GST will apply to petroleum crude, high speed diesel, petrol, natural gas and aviation turbine fuel (ATF, the fuel used by aeroplanes)

Compensation: the Council recommends compensation to States for tax income they lost because of GST, for five years. Parliament then provides for it by law: the GST (Compensation to States) Act, 2017.
Sharing income tax among the States is NOT a GST Council job. That is done on the Finance Commission's advice (Art 270, Art 280).

sections.heading: Status, disputes and the Mohit Minerals case

blocks.title: GST Council vs other bodies
head: Aspect
GST Council
Not this
rows: Constitutional body: created by Art 279A of the Constitution
It is not a statutory body (one made by an ordinary law) under the CGST Act, 2017. It was not set up by a Cabinet resolution. It is not part of the Finance Commission.
Both the Centre and the States are members (joint forum)
Not a body of the Centre alone

blocks.title: Dispute mechanism — Art 279A(11)
items: The Council sets up a mechanism to decide disputes about its recommendations or how they are carried out.
It covers only three kinds of disputes: (1) Centre vs one or more States; (2) Centre and some States on one side vs other States on the other side; (3) two or more States among themselves.
A dispute between a taxpayer and a tax officer is NOT covered. Such cases go to the GST Appellate Tribunal (GSTAT) under the CGST Act, 2017.

blocks.title: Case
head: Case (year)
Held
Why it matters
rows: Union of India v. Mohit Minerals (2022)
GST Council recommendations have only persuasive value (they guide, but need not be followed). They are NOT binding on Parliament or State Legislatures.

Art 246A gives Parliament and the State Legislatures simultaneous (equal, side-by-side) power to make GST laws, and Art 279A does not say the recommendations bind them. So being a constitutional body does not make its advice binding.

sections.heading: GST 2.0 and current facts (as of Nov 2026)

head: Item
Fact
rows: The main slabs were cut to two: 5% and 18%. The 12% and 28% slabs were removed. A special 40% rate was added for luxury and 'sin' goods (harmful goods such as tobacco; also high-end cars and yachts). The new rates applied from 22 September 2025.
Five years from 1 July 2017; ended 30 June 2022
It continued after 2022 only to repay the loans taken to pay compensation to States. It was removed on most goods from 22 September 2025 and ended fully on 1 February 2026.
GST Appellate Tribunal launched in September 2025
No GST rate was changed. The Council decided that rate changes will be taken up only once a year, from the next financial year.

blocks.text: For what replaced the compensation cess on tobacco, GSTAT deadlines and more, see Financial relations

items: The Chairperson is the Union Finance Minister. The Vice-Chairperson is chosen by the State members only.
Quorum is one-half of members (17 of 33). A decision needs three-fourths of the weighted votes of members present and voting.
The Centre has one-third weight and all States together two-thirds. Neither side alone reaches three-fourths, so neither can pass a decision alone. But the Centre alone can block one.
If the Centre votes yes, the States must give 5/8 (62.5%) of their combined vote.
The CBIC Chairperson is a permanent invitee with no vote (by a Cabinet decision). The Union Revenue Secretary is the ex-officio Secretary. The Secretariat is in New Delhi.
Ladakh is not a member (no legislature). Delhi, Puducherry and Jammu and Kashmir are members.
Constitutional body, but recommendations are NOT binding (Mohit Minerals case, 2022).
GST is a destination-based consumption tax. It came into force on 1 July 2017. Assam was the first State to ratify the GST Amendment Bill.
